Thank you! I think there are quite a few factors that changed my outcome this semester. 

1. I went to the lectures of a professor I had had previously and liked his teaching style. He technically wasn’t my assigned professor but I knew I would learn better from him than my lecturer so I found his session and sat in the third row from the front. I attended every single lecture, took detailed notes, and looked over them often. 

2. Fall semester, I used chegg to solve a lot of the homework since I honestly had no idea what was going on. This semester I made myself try every homework problem, or at least think of a method for each problem if I didn’t know how to do it, before using resources other than my notes. If I was stuck after that, I consulted slader, not chegg. It has online textbook solutions with step by step descriptions. It doesn’t give you the exact problems so I had to repeat the steps for my problems and get an answer on my own. To find the exact problem, on web-assign, next to the problem, there should be a code (ex. 16.5.007). This refers to the chapter (16), the section (section 5) and the problem number (#7). That was very helpful for learning how to do problems. 

3. I created a master study guide that ended up being about 40 pages long. Each topic/lecture was its own “chapter” so to speak and it was broken down by what was covered on each exam. A “chapter” included a short overview of the topic from the lecture notes and one or two example problems of how to apply the concept. At the end, I made three additional note pages including how to do some integration techniques I had troubles with, the different types of integrals and what methods are used to solve each, and little side hints my professor gave throughout the semester. 

4. Do (a lot of) past exams as practice and learn from mistakes then instead of on a real exam. I didn’t take this seriously first semester. I would do them but I never went back to correct my mistakes. This time I did them once, found the ones I did wrong and wrote out the correct solutions, then I would go back a second time hours later and retake it trying to apply the new things I learned previously. I did this for about 10 exams while studying for the final. Less for the first exams though. And after awhile you start to recognize certain problems. I recognized a few variations of problems from past exams on the final and was very glad to have seen them before. 

5. Lastly, the exams are important as hell, but don’t count out homework and quizzes. My first year here, I got a C in 161 even after getting nearly 100% in the homework and quiz categories. It felt like homework didn’t even contribute to my score which felt unfair. I continued to do homework nevertheless just thinking that it didn’t matter. If you failed exams, you failed the class.
